items.title: California tightens rules on AI data center energy and water use
items.description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.
Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption …
Read the full story at The Verge.
items.content: California Gov. Gavin Newsom has signed seven bills designed to prevent AI data centers from passing utility costs onto residents, as reported earlier by the Los Angeles Times. The package of laws requires the California Public Utilities Commission to introduce a new rate classification for data centers, while forcing them to pay for upgrades to local power grids and water systems.Other bills included in the package will require proposed data centers to disclose their estimated water use to local governments, along with information about energy efficiency and drought planning. They must also meet certain energy, water, and fuel consumption requirements before qualifying for a streamlined approval process. Last week, Newsom signed an executive order to speed up the creation of an AI “kill switch.”RelatedGavin Newsom is pushing for an AI kill switch“While the Trump administration moves toward deregulation, communities are left to deal with the consequences — higher electricity demand, grid constraints, water use, and pollution,” Newsom says in the press release. “With these laws, we are ensuring that Californians remain in the driver’s seat — and that those profiting from data centers aren’t doing so at our expense.”
items.author: Emma Roth
items.titleZh: 加州收紧对人工智能数据中心能源和水资源使用的规定
items.descriptionZh:
加州州长加文·纽森签署了七项法案，旨在防止AI数据中心将公用事业成本转嫁给居民。据《洛杉矶时报》此前报道，这组法律要求加州公共事业委员会（CPUC）为数据中心引入新的费率分类，并迫使数据中心为地方电网和水系统升级付费。其他法案则要求拟建数据中心向地方政府披露其预计用水量，以及能效和抗旱规划信息；数据中心还必须满足特定的能源、水和燃料消耗要求，才有资格获得简化审批。上周，纽森还签署行政命令，加快建立AI“终止开关”。

纽森在新闻稿中表示，当特朗普政府走向放松监管时，社区却要承受后果——更高的电力需求、电网限制、用水和污染。“通过这些法律，我们确保加州人继续掌握主导权——也让从数据中心获利的人不能以我们的利益为代价。”

背景是AI热潮下数据中心快速扩张。AI训练和推理依赖大量GPU/加速器集群，功率密度高，需要持续供电和冷却，通常耗电、耗水都很大。其核心运行原理决定了资源消耗：服务器密集计算产生大量热量，需制冷系统持续散热，常见水冷或蒸发冷却会消耗水资源；训练任务负荷高且集中，还会推高局部电网峰值。如果数据中心不承担相应的电网扩容、水系统改造和环境影响成本，这些费用可能通过公用事业费率由普通居民分摊。

加州这组法案的核心创新，是把数据中心的外部成本内部化：通过新的费率类别，让数据中心按其负荷和成本因果付费；通过披露和审批门槛，把用水、能效和抗旱规划纳入准入条件；通过要求支付电网和水系统升级，减少“企业获利、社区买单”的情况。这并非技术标准，而是监管和费率机制创新，但它会直接改变AI基础设施的运营约束。

从影响看，这会提高数据中心在加州的合规和运营成本，促使其更重视能效、节水冷却、现场可再生能源、储能和需求响应，也可能影响选址和扩张节奏。地方政府将获得更多用水与能效信息，便于评估项目影响。与联邦层面特朗普政府放松监管的方向相比，加州选择加强监管，形成明显政策对比。不过，原文未提供具体性能参数或量化对比数据，例如电价涨幅、用水上限、能耗门槛、受影响数据中心数量或成本节省额等，因此无法进行数值层面的比较；目前能确认的是政策机制和监管方向。

关于“AI终止开关”，新闻将其作为纽森推动AI治理的另一动作，但未展开技术细节。总体而言，这组法律标志着加州在AI基础设施监管上从被动应对转向主动设限，试图在AI产业发展与居民电费、水资源和电网负担之间重新分配责任。

items.title: NVIDIA Launches DSX Ready to Qualify Power and Cooling Products for AI Factories
items.description: Every AI factory needs power and cooling that fit its computing architecture. As AI infrastructure expands, power, cooling, water, site and grid constraints are shaping what builders can deploy. Choosing products that fit the complete factory design helps builders turn computing capacity into useful AI output. To help builders make those decisions, NVIDIA is introducing […]
items.content: Every AI factory needs power and cooling that fit its computing architecture. As AI infrastructure expands, power, cooling, water, site and grid constraints are shaping what builders can deploy. Choosing products that fit the complete factory design helps builders turn computing capacity into useful AI output. To help builders make those decisions, NVIDIA is introducing NVIDIA DSX Ready, a qualification program for partner products and solutions that meet applicable NVIDIA DSX AI factory reference design requirements. The program launches with two initial categories: battery energy storage systems (BESS) and cooling distribution units (CDUs). Category-specific requirements and review through the program help builders evaluate offerings with greater confidence, reduce integration risk and move toward deployment. Qualified Building Blocks for Building AI Factory The NVIDIA DSX AI factory platform unifies AI factory design and operations across compute, networking, power, cooling, facilities and software. It helps partners design and operate the factory as one system to produce more useful AI output within available power, cooling, water and grid constraints. That system view matters now because optimizing one part of an AI factory can shift the bottleneck elsewhere. Power and cooling suppliers need a clear path from reference designs to qualified offerings, and builders need a clearer way to discover and evaluate those offerings. DSX Ready connects that selection process to applicable NVIDIA DSX requirements. It gives builders a clear qualification to look for and gives partners a defined way to demonstrate that a specific offering meets the requirements for its category. Power and Cooling Qualification At launch, DSX Ready includes qualified BESS solutions Hitachi Energy, LG Energy Solution and Tesla, and qualified CDU solutions from LG Electronics, LiquidStack and Vertiv. These initial categories bring power systems and liquid-cooling infrastructure into a common program, with requirements tailored to each technology. Additional categories across infrastructure and software will be rolled out over time. For BESS providers, partners run the required qualification tests and submit supporting data for NVIDIA review and approval within a defined qualification boundary. Passing qualification does not replace site-level engineering or imply site-level stability. For CDU providers, the path uses the CDU self-qualification suite to determine whether a specific offering meets applicable NVIDIA functional requirements. Teams can then focus on how qualified offerings fit their site, configuration and operating needs. A qualified CDU may meet the relevant cooling criteria, for example, while the builder still evaluates how it will fit the planned facility. From Platform Design to Partner Selection The value of a reference design grows when builders can connect it to specific products and informed engineering decisions. DSX Ready makes that connection, bringing partner innovation into the infrastructure choices behind NVIDIA DSX AI factories. Explore NVIDIA DSX Ready qualification categories and learn how to participate. Connect with the right NVIDIA team to begin qualification for a product or solution.
items.author: Vishal Ganeriwala
items.descriptionZh:
随着 AI 基础设施持续扩张，电力、冷却、水、站点和电网约束正在决定 AI 工厂建设者能够部署什么。每个 AI 工厂都需要与其计算架构匹配的供电和冷却；只有选择适合完整工厂设计的产品，才能把计算容量转化为有用的 AI 输出。为此，NVIDIA 推出 NVIDIA DSX Ready，这是一项针对合作伙伴产品与解决方案的资格认证计划，目标确认相关产品满足适用的 NVIDIA DSX AI 工厂参考设计要求。计划首批覆盖两个类别：电池储能系统（BESS）和冷却分配单元（CDU）。每个类别有特定要求和审查流程，帮助建设者更有信心地评估产品、降低集成风险并推进部署。

NVIDIA DSX AI 工厂平台将 AI 工厂的设计与运营统一起来，覆盖计算、网络、供电、冷却、设施和软件。其核心理念是让合作伙伴把 AI 工厂作为一个系统来设计和运营，从而在可用电力、冷却、水与电网约束内产出更多有用 AI 输出。这一“系统级”视角在当下尤为关键，因为单独优化 AI 工厂的某个环节，可能把瓶颈转移到其他地方。电力与冷却供应商需要一条从参考设计到合格产品的清晰路径，建设者也需要更清晰的方式来发现和评估这些产品。DSX Ready 正是把选择过程与适用的 NVIDIA DSX 要求连接起来：建设者可以寻找明确的资格标识，合作伙伴则可通过定义好的方式证明某一产品满足其类别要求。

在首批类别中，DSX Ready 已纳入合格的 BESS 解决方案，来自 Hitachi Energy、LG Energy Solution 和 Tesla；合格的 CDU 解决方案来自 LG Electronics、LiquidStack 和 Vertiv。初始类别把电力系统和液冷基础设施纳入同一个计划，但要求针对不同技术分别定制。未来还将逐步推出更多基础设施和软件类别。

针对 BESS 提供商，合作伙伴需运行所需资格测试，并在明确的资格边界内提交支持数据，供 NVIDIA 审查和批准。需要强调的是，通过资格并不替代站点级工程，也不意味着站点级稳定性。针对 CDU 提供商，资格路径使用 CDU 自资格套件，判断特定产品是否满足适用的 NVIDIA 功能要求。团队随后可重点评估合格产品如何适配其站点、配置和运营需求。例如，一个合格 CDU 可能满足相关冷却标准，但建设者仍需评估它如何融入计划中的设施。

从平台设计到合作伙伴选择，参考设计的价值在建设者能够将其连接到具体产品和有依据的工程决策时才会放大。DSX Ready 建立了这种连接，把合作伙伴创新带入 NVIDIA DSX AI 工厂背后的基础设施选择。值得注意的是，本次公告未披露各产品的具体功率、容量、效率、PUE 或成本等性能参数，也未提供不同厂商产品之间的横向性能对比；其重点在于建立资格认证框架、类别要求、审查边界和参与流程。对 AI 工厂建设者而言，这意味着可在电力、冷却、水和电网受限的环境中，更早筛选经过验证的供电和冷却构建模块，降低集成不确定性，加速部署；对供应商而言，则获得了一条依据 NVIDIA DSX 参考设计展示产品合规性的明确通道。NVIDIA 表示，可进一步探索 DSX Ready 资格类别、了解参与方式，并联系相应 NVIDIA 团队为产品或解决方案启动资格认证。

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro Max storage can drop lower than a hard drive at 1.1 MB/s during heavy writes — QLC NAND offers higher capacity but reportedly suffers 38% drop compared to TLC-based Pro
items.description: Apple's use of QLC NAND allows the iPhone 18 Pro Max to offer higher storage capacity, but Homolab's testing highlights the potential performance trade-off under sustained writes.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 7 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Apple’s latest iPhone 18 Pro series went on sale last week, and the company’s decision to use QLC-based NAND for higher-capacity storage variants appears to come with a trade-off. Bilibili channel Homolab recently tested a 1TB iPhone 18 Pro Max and found that its storage performance can drop significantly under sustained heavy workloads. Since QLC stores four bits of data per memory cell when compared to three bits with TLC, it allows manufacturers to offer higher capacities using the same physical space. However, this higher storage density comes at the cost of slower performance, particularly when handling large amounts of data.Tom's Hardware Premium Roadmaps (Image credit: Future)Leading-edge foundry roadmapsNvidia Enterprise GPU and CPU roadmapAMD's Enterprise GPU and CPU roadmapIntel's roadmaps examined — 14A, Nova Lake, Diamond Rapids & AI accelerator pushCo-Packaged Optics (CPO) foundry roadmapsHomolab compared the 1TB QLC-based iPhone 18 Pro Max with a 512GB TLC-based iPhone 18 Pro. While both storage types perform fairly similarly in 4K read tests, the QLC model falls behind by 38% in a low-queue-depth mixed workload, scoring 8,168 compared to 11,285 for the TLC model. Under heavier workloads, the gap narrows, although the TLC storage model still maintains a 12% advantage.The drop in performance is even more apparent when it comes to sustained write tests. The iPhone 18 Pro Max uses a fast SLC cache that can deliver speeds of up to 3,000 MB/s. Once that cache is exhausted, a secondary TLC-based buffer takes over, averaging around 578 MB/s. When both cache buffers are exhausted, the phone has to write directly to the underlying QLC NAND. At that point, sustained write performance can fall to 79.4 MB/s, with speeds occasionally dropping as low as 25.6 MB/s.That is significantly slow and comparable to the performance of many budget microSD cards (microSD Express cards are much faster). Things look even worse once the storage starts filling up. At 60% capacity, the available SLC cache drops from 250GB to just 58GB. This also causes the secondary buffer to slow down to 396 MB/s, while direct QLC writes average just 45 MB/s and occasionally fall to as low as 1.1 MB/s.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: It’s important to note that these are synthetic benchmarks and are meant to represent a worse case scenario. Users should not experience any performance issues during typical tasks such as web browsing, messaging, gaming, or taking photos. Any slowdown is likely to be noticeable only during specific workloads, such as 4K or ProRes recording, large file transfers, or data backup restores. Having said that, testing by Homolab does point to the trade-off involved in using QLC NAND for a high-capacity flagship smartphone, particularly for users who regularly deal with storage-intensive tasks. items.titleZh: iPhone 18 Pro Max storage can drop lower than a hard drive at 1.1 MB/s during heavy writes — QLC NAND offers higher capacity but reportedly suffers 38% drop compared to TLC-based Pro
items.descriptionZh:
Tom's Hardware 报道，Apple 上周开售 iPhone 18 Pro 系列，其高容量存储版本采用基于 QLC 的 NAND 闪存，而非此前更常见的 TLC，这带来容量与性能之间的取舍。B站频道 Homolab 对 1TB iPhone 18 Pro Max 进行测试，并与 512GB TLC 版 iPhone 18 Pro 对比，发现 QLC 机型在持续重负载下存储性能会明显下降。

核心原理在于 NAND 每个存储单元保存的比特数不同：SLC 为 1 比特，TLC 为 3 比特，QLC 为 4 比特。QLC 每个单元有 16 种电平状态，而 TLC 为 8 种。因此 QLC 能在相同物理空间内提供更高容量，但写入时需要更精细的电压控制，速度更慢、出错率更高，通常也更依赖缓存和垃圾回收策略来掩盖短板。手机通常先用部分 NAND 模拟 SLC 缓存，获得极快写入；SLC 缓存耗尽后，再使用二级 TLC 缓冲；两级缓存都耗尽后，才直接写入 QLC NAND。存储占用越高，可用缓存越小，持续写入性能越差。

测试数据显示，在 4K 读取测试中，QLC 与 TLC 机型表现相近；但在低队列深度混合工作负载中，QLC 机型得分 8,168，TLC 机型得分 11,285，QLC 落后约 38%。在更重负载下，两者差距缩小，但 TLC 仍保持约 12% 优势。持续写入测试更能体现问题：1TB iPhone 18 Pro Max 的 SLC 缓存速度可达 3,000 MB/s；SLC 缓存耗尽后，二级 TLC 缓冲平均约 578 MB/s；当两级缓存都耗尽、必须直写 QLC NAND 时，持续写入速度可降至 79.4 MB/s，偶尔甚至低至 25.6 MB/s，已接近许多廉价 microSD 卡的水平，远慢于 microSD Express。存储开始填满后情况更糟：当容量用到 60%，可用 SLC 缓存从 250GB 骤降至 58GB，二级缓冲降至 396 MB/s，直写 QLC 平均仅 45 MB/s，偶尔低至 1.1 MB/s。

需要指出，这些是合成基准测试，代表较极端的最坏情况。日常网页浏览、消息、游戏、拍照等普通任务通常不会让用户感到明显问题。性能瓶颈更可能出现在 4K 或 ProRes 视频录制、大文件传输、数据备份恢复等存储密集型场景。总体来看，Apple 在高容量旗舰机型上采用 QLC，是以存储密度换取容量，适合更看重容量、写入负载不重的用户；但对经常处理大文件、高码率视频或频繁备份恢复的专业用户而言，高容量 QLC 机型可能在持续写入和缓存耗尽后明显不如 TLC 稳定。这也是 QLC 进入高端智能手机后需要面对的核心权衡。

items.title: From Enablement to Execution, Egypt’s AI Ecosystem Reaches Production Scale
items.description: Today, Egypt’s AI builders gathered in the Grand Egyptian Museum for a reception that highlighted the nation’s rapidly growing AI ecosystem — spanning AI natives, developers, researchers, startups and enterprises — building applications across industries. The event included a keynote from Paolo Guglielmini, vice president of EMEA at NVIDIA. Ahmed Mostafa, regional AI adoption lead […]
items.content: Today, Egypt’s AI builders gathered in the Grand Egyptian Museum for a reception that highlighted the nation’s rapidly growing AI ecosystem — spanning AI natives, developers, researchers, startups and enterprises — building applications across industries. The event included a keynote from Paolo Guglielmini, vice president of EMEA at NVIDIA. Ahmed Mostafa, regional AI adoption lead for the Middle East and Africa at NVIDIA, delivered a session on “Why Accelerating Every Layer Matters,” exploring NVIDIA’s full-stack approach to AI development and deployment. The event also featured a panel moderated by Basil Fateen, head of startups for the Middle East and Africa at NVIDIA, with participation from startups across smart spaces, healthcare, cybersecurity and robotics. In Egypt, the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute learner base grew more than tenfold in a single year. In June, the National Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Egypt licensed Hassan Allam Data Centers to build and operate data centers in the country. Under that license, Hassan Allam Utilities and investment firm A15 agreed to develop a new data center, an estimated $400 million investment. In addition, NVIDIA and A15 in July hosted an event connecting Egypt’s leading founders with NVIDIA’s global ecosystem. This has been complemented by recent startup and investor events in Egypt, including engagements with A15 and Plug and Play at the Creativa Innovation Hub at Sultan Hussein Kamel Palace, an affiliate of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. Spanning a range of industries, members of the NVIDIA Inception program in Egypt include: Aidera: A unified enterprise intelligence system that connects data, systems, workflows and operational touch points turning enterprise-wide signals into informed decisions, intelligent automation, coordinated execution and measurable impact. Intella: Developing Arabic speech intelligence for applications across financial services, telecommunications and more. Marses Robotics: Developing autonomous robotics and industrial automation technologies. Proteinea: Combining AI protein design with lab experiments to develop differentiated medicines. Stakpak: Developing an open source autonomous developer-operations AI agent. Paymob and Thndr: Building better financial services through technology and AI. The NVIDIA VC Alliance has also expanded its presence in Egypt, with A15 and M Empire joining the program, connecting more local investors with NVIDIA’s global startup ecosystem. This momentum has been complemented by startup and investor events, including collaborations with RiseUp and Plug and Play, as well as Flat6Labs, a regional entrepreneurship platform supporting startups and innovation across emerging markets, and Algebra Ventures, a Cairo-based venture capital firm backing technology startups. AI Growth Across Africa The Egypt ecosystem event showed just a piece of Africa’s larger, growing AI ecosystem. For most of the past decade, conversations about Africa’s AI ecosystem revolved around “potential.” They centered on what the technology might do for the continent, rather than what the continent could build with it. Africa is home to roughly 18% of the world’s population but less than 1% of the world’s data center capacity. This means African developers have often relied on cloud-based compute hosted outside the continent for large-scale AI training. This is rapidly changing. Within a year, four AI factories have been announced or brought online across Africa, with another 656 megawatts of new capacity in the pipeline. These AI factories will provide African developers and enterprises with the accelerated computing infrastructure needed to train, fine-tune and deploy AI models closer to where data is created. Cassava Technologies, Africa’s first NVIDIA Cloud Partner, is expanding access to NVIDIA accelerated computing through its AI factory in South Africa and planned deployments across Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria and Morocco — an investment that could reach $720 million. In Egypt, Cassava and Vodafone Egypt recently announced an AI factory initiative to provide businesses and government organizations with locally hosted AI infrastructure through GPU-as-a-service, supporting the development and deployment of AI applications while keeping data in-country. Building on Cassava’s first AI factory in South Africa, the rollout aims to expand access to local accelerated computing, helping developers, enterprises and researchers train, customize and deploy AI models closer to where their data is created. Similarly, Stratos Lab, a South African AI neocloud provider, is partnering with ECOBLOX and Digital Parks Africa to launch an AI cloud powered by more than 50 NVIDIA HGX B300 systems — delivering over 7 exaflops of performance. The deployment gives African enterprises and developers access to high-performance GPU compute locally, enabling model training, inference and agentic AI workloads with lower latency and at reduced costs. And at GITEX Africa in Marrakech in April, Nexus Core Systems announced a collaboration with Morocco’s Ministry of Digital Transition, its Ministry of Investment and the investment agency AMDIE to build the Nexus AI factory outside Casablanca: a $1.2 billion initial investment with 500 megawatts planned, NVIDIA Blackwell accelerated computing and renewable power from TAQA Morocco. The Demand Was Already There Infrastructure of this kind is not based on mere potential — it’s based on confidence that local developers and enterprises are ready to put the infrastructure to productive use. In 2024, NVIDIA set a target of training 100,000 developers across Africa through the NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute within three years. To date, NVIDIA’s trained over 85,000 developers in Africa, and the continent is among NVIDIA’s fastest-growing developer regions — Nigeria is now the institute’s second-largest market globally. InstaDeep joined NVIDIA Inception in 2017 as a small team in Tunis using its first NVIDIA DGX system. Since then, it’s developed drug discovery, protein design and logistics optimization applications, and was acquired by BioNTech for about $680 million. Africa accounts for roughly a third of the world’s languages, often invisible to frontier models. To help advance African language models, language model lab Lelapa AI built InkubaLM and the Vulavula speech service for South African languages including isiZulu and Sesotho. MeetKai, for example, an NVIDIA Inception member, is expanding its work in Egypt with Smart Africa, building its AI stack on NVIDIA technology as part of its plans for the market. The company is among a growing group of AI innovators using NVIDIA technology to build and scale across Africa. And there’s still much room to grow. McKinsey puts African data center demand at roughly 0.4 gigawatts today, and estimates it will rise to between 1.5 and 2.2 gigawatts by 2030, which requires between $10 to $20 billion in construction. Learn more about the NVIDIA Developer Program, NVIDIA Inception and NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute.

items.titleZh: 从赋能到执行，埃及的人工智能生态系统达到生产规模
items.descriptionZh:
英伟达在埃及大埃及博物馆举办了一场接待活动，集中展示埃及快速成长的AI生态：参与者覆盖AI原生企业、开发者、研究者、初创公司与行业企业，应用横跨多个行业。英伟达EMEA副总裁Paolo Guglielmini发表主题演讲；英伟达中东和非洲区域AI采用负责人Ahmed Mostafa以“为什么加速每一层都很重要”为题，介绍英伟达面向AI开发与部署的全栈方法。活动还设有由英伟达中东和非洲初创业务负责人Basil Fateen主持的圆桌，参与初创企业来自智能空间、医疗健康、网络安全和机器人等领域。

在埃及，英伟达深度学习学院（DLI）的学习者规模一年内增长超过十倍。今年6月，埃及国家电信监管局向Hassan Allam Data Centers发放许可，允许其在埃及建设和运营数据中心。根据该许可，Hassan Allam Utilities与投资公司A15同意开发一座新数据中心，预计投资约4亿美元。7月，英伟达与A15还举办活动，将埃及领先创始人与英伟达全球生态连接起来。近期埃及还举行了多场初创与投资者活动，包括在通信与信息技术部下属的Sultan Hussein Kamel Palace的Creativa Innovation Hub与A15、Plug and Play的互动。

英伟达Inception计划在埃及的成员覆盖多个行业：Aidera提供统一企业智能系统，连接数据、系统、工作流和运营触点，将企业信号转化为决策、智能自动化、协同执行和可衡量影响；Intella开发面向金融服务、电信等场景的阿拉伯语语音智能；Marses Robotics研发自主机器人与工业自动化技术；Proteinea将AI蛋白质设计与实验室实验结合，开发差异化药物；Stakpak开发开源自主开发者运维AI代理；Paymob和Thndr则通过技术与AI改进金融服务。英伟达VC Alliance也在埃及扩展，A15和M Empire加入该计划，把更多本地投资者连接到英伟达全球初创生态。相关势头还得到RiseUp、Plug and Play、Flat6Labs以及开罗风投机构Algebra Ventures等活动的配合。

这场埃及生态活动只是非洲更大AI生态成长的一部分。过去十年，非洲AI讨论多围绕“潜力”，关注技术能为非洲做什么，而不是非洲能用技术构建什么。非洲拥有全球约18%的人口，却只占全球不到1%的数据中心容量，因此非洲开发者过去常依赖非洲以外的云端算力进行大规模AI训练。这一局面正在迅速改变：一年内，非洲已有四座AI工厂宣布或上线，另有656兆瓦新容量在管线中。这些AI工厂将为非洲开发者和企业提供加速计算基础设施，使其能在数据产生地附近训练、微调和部署AI模型。

非洲首家英伟达云合作伙伴Cassava Technologies正通过其南非AI工厂以及在埃及、肯尼亚、尼日利亚和摩洛哥的规划部署，扩大英伟达加速计算的可及性，投资规模可能达到7.2亿美元。在埃及，Cassava与Vodafone Egypt近期宣布AI工厂计划，通过GPU即服务为企业和政府机构提供本地托管的AI基础设施，支持AI应用开发与部署，同时将数据留在境内。南非AI新云提供商Stratos Lab则与ECOBLOX和Digital Parks Africa合作，推出由50多套英伟达HGX B300系统驱动的AI云，提供超过7 exaflops性能。该部署让非洲企业和开发者获得本地高性能GPU算力，以更低延迟和成本支持模型训练、推理和代理式AI工作负载。4月在马拉喀什GITEX Africa上，Nexus Core Systems宣布与摩洛哥数字转型部、投资部及投资机构AMDIE合作，在卡萨布兰卡郊外建设Nexus AI工厂：初期投资12亿美元，规划500兆瓦，采用英伟达Blackwell加速计算，并由TAQA Morocco提供可再生电力。

这类基础设施并非仅基于潜力，而是基于对本地开发者和企业已准备好有效使用算力的信心。2024年，英伟达设定目标：三年内通过DLI在非洲培训10万名开发者。截至目前，英伟达已在非洲培训超过8.5万名开发者，非洲是英伟达增长最快的开发者地区之一，尼日利亚已成为DLI全球第二大市场。InstaDeep于2017年以突尼斯小型团队身份加入英伟达Inception，使用其首套英伟达DGX系统，此后开发了药物发现、蛋白质设计和物流优化应用，并被BioNTech以约6.8亿美元收购。非洲拥有全球约三分之一语言，这些语言常在前沿模型中不可见。为推进非洲语言模型，语言模型实验室Lelapa AI构建了InkubaLM和Vulavula语音服务，覆盖isiZulu、Sesotho等南非语言。英伟达Inception成员MeetKai正与Smart Africa扩大在埃及的业务，基于英伟达技术构建AI栈，以推进其市场计划。越来越多AI创新者正使用英伟达技术在非洲构建和扩展业务。增长空间仍然很大：麦肯锡估计，非洲当前数据中心需求约0.4吉瓦，到2030年将升至1.5至2.2吉瓦，需要100亿至200亿美元建设投资。

从技术角度看，英伟达强调的“加速每一层”并非单点GPU优化，而是全栈加速：从底层加速计算平台、系统与网络，到CUDA-X库、AI框架和软件栈，再到上层模型、代理式AI与行业应用，各层都针对AI负载优化，以提升训练、微调、推理和部署效率。AI工厂则可理解为面向AI生产的专门化数据中心，通过本地化加速算力、GPU即服务和Blackwell/HGX等新一代系统，降低延迟与成本，并支持数据主权。其影响在于：埃及和非洲正从AI“消费者”转向AI“生产者”，在金融、医疗、语言、机器人、网络安全、药物研发和工业自动化等领域形成本地化应用，同时吸引投资、培育开发者并完善算力基础设施。

items.title: AMD Ryzen 5 5500F and 7500 show up at retail with pricing above MSRP — budget CPUs are $20 more expensive than list price, even from first-party sellers
items.description: Nearly two weeks after they were announced, AMD's Ryzen 5 5500F and 7500 (non-F) are available for sale, though prices are slightly above MSRP.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter AMD's new Ryzen 5 5500F and Ryzen 5 7500 are available for sale, though the prices are higher than AMD originally suggested. On Amazon, the Ryzen 5 5500F is available for $120, while the Ryzen 5 7500 is listed at $210, both $20 more expensive than AMD's suggested retail pricing. Both are sold directly by Amazon, suggesting we'll see slightly higher prices for these two chips than AMD originally suggested.Get the AMD Ryzen 5 5500F from AmazonGet the AMD Ryzen 5 7500 from AmazonAMD revealed the budget CPUs nearly two weeks ago, and despite launching on that date, the chips haven't been available for sale in the U.S. until now. The Ryzen 5 5500F is particularly interesting, as the $90 Ryzen 5 5500 has continually been among Amazon's best sellers in CPUs. Although the Ryzen 5 5500 and 5500F sound similar, there are actually quite a few differences between the two CPUs.Both are six-core, 12-thread chips using AMD's Zen 3 architecture, but the 5500 falls under the Cezanne family, while the 5500F falls under Vermeer. The 5500F comes with PCIe 4, compared to PCIe 3 on the 5500, as well as a higher 4.4 GHz boost clock — the base 5500 tops out at 4.2 GHz. These changes apparently allow the 5500F to achieve higher performance, somewhere in the range of 5% to 10%, in games. We'll be getting the CPU in the Tom's Hardware lab to test the performance ourselves.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Although Zen 3 is aging, it has become an ideal home for budget builders as the RAM pricing crisis continues to surge. In addition to the Ryzen 5 5500F, we saw AMD re-release the Ryzen 7 5800X3D earlier this year to combat rising DDR5 prices. Image 1 of 1 (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Image 1 of 1 View Original We took the Ryzen 5 5500 (non-F) out for a spin earlier this year for a budget $100 CPU shootout. Generally, it underperforms the Intel competition at this price, but a 5% to 10% jump would close that gap. If performance holds up, the Ryzen 5 5500F may have a shot at our best CPUs for gaming list with its low price.The Ryzen 5 7500 is easier to parse. It's identical to the 7500F, just with integrated graphics. It comes with six Zen 4 cores for a total of 12 threads, and unlike the 5500, it exclusively supports DDR5 memory. The 7500 comes with a boost clock of 5 GHz and supports PCIe 5. Like the 5500F, it has a 65W TDP and comes bundled with AMD's Wraith Stealth cooler.AMD originally announced the Ryzen 5 5500F at $99 and the 7500 at $190, though the current Amazon listings are both $20 higher than that — $120 and $210, respectively. At the time of writing, the CPUs are only available at Amazon in the U.S.; Micro Center and Newegg don't have listings available. When other retailers pick up the chips, prices could come down.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsThis isn't the first time we've seen oddly high prices on new AMD releases at Amazon. Earlier this year, the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 went up for sale on Amazon prior to release, selling for $1,000, $100 above MSRP. After the launch dust settled and listings went up at other retailers, the pricing dropped back down to $900. Hopefully, we'll see something similar happen here. items.titleZh: AMD Ryzen 5 5500F and 7500 show up at retail with pricing above MSRP — budget CPUs are $20 more expensive than list price, even from first-party sellers
items.descriptionZh:
AMD新款入门级处理器Ryzen 5 5500F和Ryzen 5 7500已在美国亚马逊正式开售，但实际售价均高于AMD最初公布的建议零售价。其中Ryzen 5 5500F标价120美元，Ryzen 5 7500标价210美元，分别比官方建议价99美元和190美元高出20美元。两款产品目前均由亚马逊直接销售，且仅亚马逊有货，Micro Center和Newegg尚未上架。AMD大约两周前发布了这两款芯片，但直到现在才在美国市场铺货。当其他零售商开始销售后，价格有望回落。

Ryzen 5 5500F尤其值得关注，因为此前售价90美元的Ryzen 5 5500长期位居亚马逊CPU畅销榜。虽然名称相近，但5500F与5500存在显著差异。两者均为6核12线程、基于Zen 3架构，但5500属于Cezanne家族，而5500F属于Vermeer家族。5500F支持PCIe 4.0，而5500仅支持PCIe 3.0；5500F的加速频率提升至4.4 GHz，5500最高为4.2 GHz。这些改进使5500F在游戏中的性能提升约5%至10%。Tom's Hardware实验室将对其进行实测。在当前内存价格持续飙升的背景下，尽管Zen 3架构已显老旧，但它已成为预算装机者的理想选择。除5500F外，AMD今年早些时候还重新发布了Ryzen 7 5800X3D，以应对DDR5内存涨价。Tom's Hardware此前曾对Ryzen 5 5500进行过100美元级CPU对比测试，结果显示其性能通常不敌同价位英特尔竞品，但若5500F能实现5%至10%的提升，将有望缩小这一差距。如果性能表现稳定，凭借低廉价格，5500F有望跻身最佳游戏CPU榜单。

Ryzen 5 7500的定位则更为清晰。它本质上与7500F相同，只是增加了集成显卡。该芯片采用6个Zen 4核心，共12线程，仅支持DDR5内存，加速频率达5 GHz，并支持PCIe 5.0。与5500F一样，其TDP为65W，附赠AMD Wraith Stealth散热器。

价格方面，AMD最初宣布5500F为99美元、7500为190美元，但当前亚马逊售价均高出20美元。截至发稿，这两款CPU仅在美国亚马逊有售。这并非亚马逊首次出现AMD新品定价异常：今年早些时候，Ryzen 9 9950X3D2在正式发布前便以1000美元上架，比建议零售价高100美元，待其他零售商跟进后价格回落至900美元。此次情况或许类似。总体而言，5500F为仍在使用DDR4的预算玩家提供了更具性价比的升级选择，而7500则面向希望以较低成本进入DDR5/AM5平台的入门用户，两款产品在内存价格高企的当下各有明确的应用场景。

items.title: Huawei shelves global AI chip rollout as China's own demand outstrips supply — 15,488-chip Atlas clusters leverage optical networking to counter Nvidia, scales to 120 EFLOPS
items.description: Huawei says it will not offer its latest AI hardware outside of China citing lack of capacity to serve domestic demand.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 0 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Huawei's impressive next-generation Ascend 900-series AI accelerators will be offered only in China, not internationally, as the company struggles to meet domestic demand amid capacity constraints, the company announced this week. While the upcoming Ascend 960-series neural processing units (NPUs) could rival some of AMD's and Nvidia's existing AI GPUs, demand for these units outside of China was not guaranteed anyway.Go deeper with TH Premium: AI shortages (Image credit: Nvidia)AI data centers are swallowing the world's memory and storage supplyDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleChip scarcity assaults auto industry amid the worsening Nexperia and DRAM crisisThe custom AI ASIC state of play"Since we do not have enough capacity to even satisfy the ​demand in China, we do not have a plan to expand into the international market in a fully-fledged way," said Eric Xu, rotating chairman of Huawei, on the sidelines of the company's Huawei Connect conference, Reuters reports. He added that Huawei supplies limited volumes to 'some countries where demand is particularly strong,' though he did not elaborate.Huawei this week unveiled its latest AI accelerator roadmap, revealing major training and inference performance gains for its next-generation Ascend 960, 970, and 980 NPUs over the existing Ascend 910C and Ascend 950-series. The Ascend 960DT and 960PR are set to increase their FP8 training performance to 2 PFLOPS and their FP4 inference performance to 4 PFLOPS and 8 PFLOPS, respectively, in 2027. Meanwhile, their successors, Ascend 970 and Ascend 980, are projected to increase their FP4 performance to 14 PFLOPS and 28 PFLOPS, respectively, in the coming years.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Huawei Ascend vs Nvidia AI GPUs Swipe to scroll horizontally NPU FP8 Performance FP4 Perf Memory Memory Bandwidth Interconnect Bandwidth Targeted Release Nvidia H200 4 PFLOPS - 141 GB HBM3E 4.8 TB/s 900 GB/s 2023 Q4 Nvidia B300 10 PFLOPS 15/20 S/D PFLOPS 279 GB HBM3E 8 TB/s 1.8 TB/s 2025 Q4 Ascend 950PR 1 PFLOPS 2 PFLOPS 128 GB of HiBL 1.0 1.6 TB/s 2 TB/s 2026 Q1 Ascend 950DT 1 PFLOPS 2 PFLOPS 144 GB of HiZQ 2.0 4.0 TB/s 2 TB/s 2026 Q4 Nvidia R200 17.5 PFLOPS 35/50 T/I PFLOPS 288 GB HBM4 19.2 TB/s 3 TB/s 2026 Q4 Ascend 960DT 2 PFLOPS 4 PFLOPS 288 GB 9.6 TB/s 2.2 TB/s 2027 Q1 Ascend 960PR 2 PFLOPS 8 PFLOPS 192 GB 2.4 TB/s 2.2 TB/s 2027 Q3 Ascend 970 3.6 PFLOPS 14 PFLOPS 288 GB 14.4 TB/s 4.4 TB/s 2028 Ascend 980 7.2 PFLOPS* 28 PFLOPS* 384 GB 38.4 TB/s* 8 TB/s 2029 *Preliminary dataS/D - Sparse and DenseT/I - Training and InferenceBut while the upcoming Ascend NPUs will be considerably faster than their predecessors, particularly for inference, they will remain well behind Nvidia's previous- and current-generation accelerators, at least in raw compute performance. Huawei's 2027 Ascend 960DT is projected to deliver 2 FP8 TFLOPS for training, compared with Nvidia's 4 FP8 TFLOPS for the H200, released in 2023. The Ascend 960PR is expected to offer 8 FP4 PFLOPS for training, which is far behind Nvidia's B300, which delivers 15–20 NVFP4 PFLOPS. Even the Ascend 980, targeted for 2029, is projected to reach 7.2 FP8 PFLOPS and 28 FP4 PFLOPS, well below Nvidia's R200, which is on track to deliver 17.5 FP8 PFLOPS and 35/50 FP4 PFLOPS this year. You may like China’s Huawei to enter South Korean AI chip market with new Atlas SuperPods, clusters pack 8,192 Ascend 950 accelerators per deployment China's homegrown AI accelerators to supply 90% of the country's domestic market, analysts suggest Huawei details AI accelerator roadmap, pulls in next-generation Ascend NPUs by several quarters Such a massive performance difference with leading AI hardware will reinforce Huawei's reliance on massive system-level scaling rather than chip-for-chip performance to compete with Nvidia. But massive system-level scaling comes with massive power consumption, which will make Huawei's next-generation Atlas SuperPoDs and SuperClusters considerably less competitive in markets that can access hardware from AMD or Nvidia.Huawei is in an interesting paradoxical situation. On the one hand, its integration efforts like near-package optics (NPO) clearly free up capacity on 'older' nodes that can be used for other components of AI platforms. But on the other hand, SMIC's inability to ramp production on 7nm and 6nm-class nodes limits Huawei's ability to supply its AI hardware anyway, which is why it can barely meet demand.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsThen again, while Huawei's Atlas SuperPoDs with up to 15,488 Ascend 960 NPUs can deliver up to 30 FP8 EFLOPS and 120 FP4 EFLOPS performance by far exceeding the capabilities of Nvidia's NVL72 clusters with a 72-GPU scale-up world size, their performance-per-watt is poised to be dramatically lower compared to Nvidia's architectures, which means that demand for such hardware outside of China will be limited at best. That said, a global AI hardware push doesn't make much sense for Huawei right now. What perhaps does make sense is offering cloud access to its hardware to various academic and research customers to popularize its CANN software stack. items.titleZh: 华为搁置全球AI芯片推广计划，因中国本土需求已超供应——15,488芯片Atlas集群利用光网络对抗英伟达，算力可扩展至120 EFLOPS
items.descriptionZh:
华为本周宣布，其下一代Ascend 900系列AI加速器将仅在中国市场销售，不向国际推广。原因在于产能限制使其难以满足国内需求。华为轮值董事长徐直军在华为Connect大会期间对路透表示：“我们没有足够产能满足中国需求，因此没有计划全面拓展国际市场。”他补充说，华为仅向“需求特别强劲的一些国家”供应有限数量，但未详细说明。尽管即将推出的Ascend 960系列NPU可能在性能上媲美AMD和Nvidia的部分现有AI GPU，但海外需求本身并无保障。

华为公布了最新AI加速器路线图，显示下一代Ascend 960、970和980 NPU相比现有Ascend 910C和950系列在训练和推理性能上有显著提升。2027年，Ascend 960DT和960PR的FP8训练性能将提升至2 PFLOPS，FP4推理性能分别达到4 PFLOPS和8 PFLOPS。后续Ascend 970和980的FP4性能预计分别提升至14 PFLOPS和28 PFLOPS。对比表格显示，Nvidia H200（2023年四季度）FP8性能为4 PFLOPS，内存141 GB HBM3E，带宽4.8 TB/s；B300（2025年四季度）FP8为10 PFLOPS，FP4为15/20（稀疏/密集）PFLOPS，内存279 GB HBM3E，带宽8 TB/s；R200（2026年四季度）FP8为17.5 PFLOPS，FP4为35/50（训练/推理）PFLOPS，内存288 GB HBM4，带宽19.2 TB/s。华为Ascend 950PR/DT（2026年）FP8为1 PFLOPS，FP4为2 PFLOPS，内存分别为128 GB HiBL 1.0和144 GB HiZQ 2.0，带宽1.6/4.0 TB/s，互联2 TB/s。Ascend 960DT（2027年一季度）FP8 2 PFLOPS，FP4 4 PFLOPS，内存288 GB，带宽9.6 TB/s，互联2.2 TB/s；960PR（2027年三季度）FP8 2 PFLOPS，FP4 8 PFLOPS，内存192 GB，带宽2.4 TB/s，互联2.2 TB/s。Ascend 970（2028年）FP8 3.6 PFLOPS，FP4 14 PFLOPS，内存288 GB，带宽14.4 TB/s，互联4.4 TB/s；Ascend 980（2029年，初步数据）FP8 7.2 PFLOPS，FP4 28 PFLOPS，内存384 GB，带宽38.4 TB/s，互联8 TB/s。

尽管代际提升明显，尤其推理性能，但华为Ascend NPU在原始计算性能上仍远落后于Nvidia的前代和当前代加速器。例如，2027年Ascend 960DT的FP8训练性能为2 PFLOPS，而2023年发布的Nvidia H200为4 PFLOPS；960PR的FP4训练性能为8 PFLOPS，远低于Nvidia B300的15-20 NVFP4 PFLOPS；即便是2029年目标中的Ascend 980，预计FP8 7.2 PFLOPS、FP4 28 PFLOPS，也低于Nvidia R200的17.5 FP8 PFLOPS和35/50 FP4 PFLOPS。这种巨大性能差距强化了华为依赖大规模系统级扩展而非单芯片性能与Nvidia竞争的策略。但大规模系统级扩展带来巨大功耗，使华为下一代Atlas SuperPoDs和SuperClusters在能够获取AMD或Nvidia硬件的市场上竞争力明显降低。

华为处于一个矛盾境地。一方面，近封装光学（NPO）等集成努力释放了“较老”节点的产能，可用于AI平台其他组件；另一方面，中芯国际无法提升7nm和6nm级节点产量，限制了华为供应AI硬件的能力，这也是其难以满足需求的原因。华为Atlas SuperPoDs最多可集成15,488个Ascend 960 NPU，提供高达30 FP8 EFLOPS和120 FP4 EFLOPS性能，远超Nvidia NVL72集群（72 GPU规模），但其每瓦性能远低于Nvidia架构，意味着海外需求最多有限。目前，全球AI硬件推广对华为意义不大。更合理的做法可能是向各类学术和研究客户提供云访问，以推广其CANN软件栈。

在中国市场，华为Ascend芯片是替代受美国出口管制影响的Nvidia高端AI芯片的关键方案，用于AI训练和推理，支持大模型。分析师认为，中国本土AI加速器将供应90%的国内市场。但产能瓶颈——尤其是中芯国际先进制程——仍是华为满足国内需求的主要制约。华为通过系统级扩展和软件生态（CANN）来弥补单芯片性能差距，并优先保障国内供应。

items.title: Can John Ternus find Apple’s next big thing?
items.description:
Today, I’m talking with Mark Gurman, who is the world’s best-sourced Apple reporter — both as Bloomberg’s chief Apple correspondent and the host of the upcoming podcast Power On. 
Earlier this month, Apple hosted its annual iPhone hardware event, virtually every detail of which was reported ahead of time by Mark. But this event was special, for a number of reasons. 
It was new Apple CEO John Ternus’ first major product launch since he took over for former CEO Tim Cook less than two weeks prior. It was also the debut of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable smartphone. The timing of those two things was not at all coincidental, as you’ll hear Mark explain. Apple takes these hardware events — and the stories they tell — extremely seriously. 
This year’s story actually says a great deal about what’s happening at Apple, how Cook managed in wholesale leadership ranks over the past year, and how all of that might change Apple’s culture. Furthermore, what all that tells about Ternus’ plan to navigate Apple from what you might call the iPhone era into the AI era.
Okay: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman on the future of Apple. Here we go.


This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. 
Mark Gurman, you’re the chief Apple correspondent and the managing editor of consumer technology at Bloomberg. Welcome to Decoder.
Good to be here finally. Thanks for having me. And it’s been a while, so it’s good to catch up on all things Apple.
Yeah, I’m really excited to talk to you. Obviously, Apple just had its big event. They announced the iPhone Duo. It was John Ternus’s first event as CEO. This is a Decoder episode, so we’ve got a new CEO, and we’ve got a new org chart inside of Apple.
There’s been a lot of shuffling. You’ve been chronicling them very, very deeply over the past few years. Let’s just start with the event. I have a very basic question for you.
Sure.
Do you ever get nostalgic for a time when you didn’t know what was going to happen at the iPhone event?
Do I ever get nostalgic? 
Do you ever wish that you, Mark Gurman, were about to be surprised?
Honestly, I never think about it that way. I’m just fixated on delivering the goods and delivering the news. And people love their Apple. People want to know everything that’s coming down to the last minute, so I’m here to provide it for them. 
The thing with me, and I don’t know if most people know this about me, but I hope people know this about me, is that I’m a huge Apple fan through and through, and I’ve always been. And I’m so lucky to be able to cover a company that I love, a company that I am obsessed with, and a company whose products I use. There are so many people who cover companies that they couldn’t care less about. That’s not me. 
So I do what I do because I love Apple and I love covering Apple. I love the community around it, and I love talking about it. And it’s always fun to get a peek at the future and help keep not only myself informed, but people informed around me.
That actually leads me to a lot of things because I’ve known you forever. We’ve been working in and around the same spaces forever. You got your start as an Apple blogger at the Apple rumor sites. 
There’s a whole culture around Apple that has grown up and changed over the years, and you can trace it to different eras of hardware, to different CEOs, to different sizes of the company. This was the first event with John Ternus as CEO. Apple announced a big new product in the iPhone Duo.
Do you sense that the community is changing? How do you think that community has changed over the years? And do you think Ternus is going to lead to a difference in what that community feels like?
I have to say, this event really didn’t feel much different than a Tim Cook event. They felt pretty interchangeable. It could have been Tim up there introducing it. It could have been Ternus up there introducing it.
The one thing I will say that did feel slightly different is that Ternus came out swinging with a point of view on AI. The first thing he came out with was about the intelligent personal hub. Now, here’s the big difference between Tim Cook and John Ternus in terms of their management style. You’re inside Apple, you’re an executive, you’ll come to him with an idea, you’ll come to him with a viewpoint, a decision, an opinion, and he’ll just pepper you with more questions. He won’t make a singular decision in many cases. It’s very much communal decision-making, collaborative decision-making. 
John Ternus, if you come to him and you want him to make a decision, he’ll make a decision. He’ll have an opinion. Now, you may hate his opinion; you may completely disagree with him, but he has a viewpoint. But that’s the big difference between talking to people about Ternus and Tim.
Ternus comes out talking about his view on AI. I may disagree with it. A lot of people may disagree with it. They may think the OpenAI or Anthropic approach is superior, but at least he came out and had a viewpoint. 
Apple’s been at this AI game now for two years since they launched Apple Intelligence at WWDC in 2024, and it’s been a mishmash of things. They haven’t really come out with a very strong narrative and viewpoint, and they finally did. So, as I said, whether you agree with it or not, they did do that. And I thought that was a really interesting way to kick off the keynote.
All right, we’re just going to get into the weeds of Apple nerds disagreeing about things. 
Okay, let’s do it.
I sat through that event, and I appreciated the same thing that you saw, which is, “Oh, we’re telling a story.” John Ternus is on the stage, and the first thing he’s doing is telling a story about this product and how it fits into the universe of technology. And then I took a beat, and I was like, oh, but they’re also just making sure that he’s successful at his first event by playing Apple’s greatest hits. 
Because an “intelligent personal hub” is just a replay of Steve Jobs saying the iMac was the digital hub. At the very end of the event, Ternus said, “There’s one more thing, and it’s the iPhone Duo.” 
There was just a part of all of that that, to me, felt like Apple saying, “Look, our new CEO can put on the clothes of the old CEO. He can do this same dance that you’re expecting.” Underneath it, what I felt was, to your point, that I don’t buy the story about the intelligent hub. 
No, I don’t buy it either.
Because any of the things we’re seeing AI do are happening in cloud services. It’s the same week that Meta launched Muse, right?
Right.
You can feel what you want about Meta launching Muse, but Mark Zuckerberg is giving everybody 8GB of storage and 8GB of RAM in the cloud, and Muse can go do a lot of things that AI on the iPhone absolutely cannot do at this point in time. 
I just felt like there was a part where they were playing it really safe with John by having him basically show up and be the new lead singer of Journey. You can’t get it wrong if you’re going to do “Lights.” If you’re going to show up on stage and do “Don’t Stop Believin’,” you’re going to be fine for a minute. And it’s all the stuff that comes after that’s going to really show his real personality. But it sounds like you thought that that’s his point of view.
Well, it’s a couple of things. At a very high level, Apple’s going to tell a story around what they have. If Apple invented ChatGPT, they would’ve invented ChatGPT, and they would’ve told a good story around that. Apple has gone as far as it’s able to, at least for now, on AI. So it’s telling the story, the best version of that story that they can with what they have to work with, with the bird they have in hand. So that’s the one thing.
I agree with you on the intelligent personal hub, and how that compares to the iMac back in ’98. And it feels like they’re trying to sell this pivot from the Mac as the center of everything with the peripherals around it; then you got to iCloud in 2011, the center of everything with the peripherals around it. Now, it’s this Intelligence right at the center with everything around it.
But what’s so fascinating is that Apple held a major product launch event in September of the year 2026 and did not introduce a single notable new AI feature. The first 15 minutes or so of the keynote was simply a replay, a re-narrativization of what they introduced over the past two years with Apple Intelligence. And so they tried to just tell that story in a more concrete way.
The other thing is they don’t have any AI devices at the very core, and so they need to prop up the iPhone as their AI device because they don’t have an alternative. But of course they’re only going to do that until they have that killer device, and then they’re going to change that whole narrative. 
So it’s a very narrative PR and marketing-driven company. And I’m not saying that to be critical. I mean, if I ran the company, obviously I’m going to tout what I have. I’m not going to veer from that. But it is interesting how they’re playing this. And I agree, they did play it very safe. There’s nothing safer than John Ternus introducing a new iPhone. It’s like the safest thing you can do. No major new AI product, no smart home hub, nothing in the spatial space, just straight down the middle.
Yeah, it seems like that next wave of smart home products, which we’re expecting later this year… I say, “We’re expecting.” I’m expecting it because that is something you have reported.
[Laughs] I am expecting it, yes.
Mark Gurman is expecting new products from Apple. That is the first cut at some truly AI-native devices. Because you have Siri AI and it is functional now in a way that it previously was not functional, you can try some new classes of devices.
There are about a half dozen AI-native devices coming in the next year and a half or so. The first will be the smart home hub, which is basically an Amazon Echo Show but Apple-style. It will have a square screen and an entirely new operating system. The idea is: what would a Siri AI operating system look like? This is that: intercom, video conferencing, proactive intelligence. 
So you walk up to it, it recognizes who you are, and it will show content personal to you. It will know who is speaking. Obviously, the Amazon Echo can do that, but Apple’s doing it in its own Apple-y way with AI-based Face ID.
They’re working on a home security system. They’re working on another version of the smart home hub that I just talked about that is attached to a robotic arm. So you put it on your desk, and it can move around. It’s actually a category that’s pretty popping in Asia and in China right now. 
Then you’ve got the wearables, the smart glasses. I still believe those are going to be introduced and shipped in 2027, so not too far from now. Trust me, you’ll be wearing them. Within 365 days, you will be wearing them and have video footage of you wearing them at the Steve Jobs Theater. And if that is not the case, either something went horribly wrong for you or something went horribly wrong for Apple.
You’ll also have the AirPods with cameras. That’s an interesting thing that we should talk about, but they’ll have the AirPods with cameras and then a few other wearables that I won’t get into.
So this is what I was talking about when I said there were eras at Apple and people’s relationship with the company really changed. The Steve Jobs era was defined by devices, and in particular, Steve Jobs himself getting up and doing a keynote and famously putting up pictures of all the existing smartphones and saying, “Well, these all suck. And here’s the reason they all suck, and here’s the iPhone and here’s why it’s better.” 
That created one kind of relationship between Apple’s enormous community of fans, its leader, and the products. I think that was very successful. I think the Tim Cook era has been meaningfully different. I think it’s largely a story about scale. To some extent, it’s a story about values. To a huge extent, it’s a story about privacy. 
Apple has marketed itself as the privacy company. It fought the FBI to keep the iPhone encrypted. There’s a lot there with Tim Cook’s version of the company, but it’s more corporate. Certainly, it’s just a vaster company. It’s safer. It’s not as rough around the edges as Jobs’ Apple, but it wasn’t as device-based. 
I don’t think the Vision Pro has the same kind of mainstream cultural impact as even the hockey puck mouse that Jobs put out. There was a thing that he could do with products that Tim Cook Apple could not quite do with products. And that just feels really different to me.
I’m going to correct you on that because every time I put an article or a post out about the Vision Pro being on life support, I get what amounts to basically a notch or two below a death threat from dozens of people. So people are passionate about it. 
Dozens? Dozens?
Well, honestly, I think what it is is that people have created businesses around spatial computing and apps, and they’re just pissed off that they’ve invested all this time and money in a category that’s probably going to die out.


And then you have consumers who spent four grand on this product, and they’re like, “I saved up for this thing, I’m living with this thing, and I’m pissed off to hear the realities.” But if you have another hour, we can talk about the Vision Pro. 
No, the comparison there is good. People have invested in it. They care deeply about it. The comparison I’m making is that the relationship people have to Apple in the Cook era is as an institution. It’s just like this big thing that spans the globe on a massive scale. 
It’s IBM.
Yeah, and in the Jobs era, it was all about really, really innovative new products that redefined categories over and over again. You’re describing a whole bunch of new products that came up in the Cook era that John Ternus is going to launch. How do you expect the culture of Apple to change around its products or its relationship to the culture to change as we go from one CEO to another?
But think about what they did. You’ve got the coolest new iPhone and Apple product in maybe 10, 20 years introduced one week after Tim Cook steps down. And then for the next 12 to 18 months, you’ve got, I don’t know, six or seven new product categories. Maybe you have 25 pretty breakthrough things. 
So Tim Cook made a decision that, even though his tenure at a product company was pretty limited in major new things, the Apple Watch turned out to be a success, even though it started as a complete dud, as you remember. The AirPods are a unique beast in that they’re an accessory, but it’s not a platform on its own yet. It’s going to get there. And the Vision Pro is a failure. 
Tim Cook could have ended his tenure as CEO with the iPhone Duo. He could have just waited. Typical transitions at Apple happen mid-October or mid-April; they happen on January 1st. It was a specific decision that was made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce the iPhone Duo. It was a specific decision made for John Ternus to be the one to introduce this whole new product roadmap. Even though, as you know, because of the length of hardware development cycles and R&D, these things were in the oven for five to 10 years.
So it’s really interesting that this decision was made to let Ternus be the face of this whole new era of products rather than allow Tim Cook to take the credit for it. And I think that’s to your point where they’re trying to draw the line in the sand of this new era. If Cook is already going to step down in the next three years, let’s just do it now and let Ternus take the credit for everything.
Take me inside that. You’ve obviously done a lot of reporting. I think you were the first to break the news that Cook would be searching for a successor. You were, I think, among the very first to break that it would be Ternus. Tell me about that process. 
This is a big decision; Cook is going to play a huge role at the company. He has a massive compensation program tied pretty much to having to talk to Xi Jinping and Donald Trump. It seems like that’s his job: to just manage that relationship. 
For $47 million a year, I would talk to Trump and Xi Jinping on the phone every day.
[Laughs] I would need at least 50, but that’s just me. That’s his job: to go do politics much the same way that Eric Schmidt at Google was in charge of governments after Larry Page became CEO. There’s a whole pattern here. 
Brad Smith at Microsoft, even though he wasn’t CEO, but yeah.
He’s the president of the company. Yeah, there’s a parallel here. Tell me about this decision of Tim Cook wanting to elevate his position to something like that, and of making John Ternus the face of the product side of the company in this new role.
So 2023 rolls around and Tim Cook starts every executive team meeting, all high-level meetings with people at Apple at the executive levels, with, “We need to start taking succession seriously. We need to start thinking about who the next people are.” At that time, there was a really strong realization that many of the people at the top of Apple either had half a billion dollars in the bank or were already billionaires, and that this era would start to age out really quickly. 
And so Tim Cook knew that he wanted to take a step back. Jeff Williams, the number two as the COO, knew he wanted to retire. The CFO, Luca Maestri, wanted to retire, too. The general counsel, Kate Adams, also wanted to retire. They were all about the same age, give or take a few years. So they basically came up with this plan that would go one by one over the next few years.
It started with the CFO. Luca retires at the very end of 2024, and he’s replaced by the new CFO, Kevan Parekh. Then 2025 rolls around, and Jeff Williams, the COO, retires and is replaced by his deputy, Sabih Khan. Then in 2026, they had the transition for the general counsel, and they got a great replacement for her from Meta, Jennifer Newstead. And then at the end of 2026, the big one: Tim Cook to John Ternus. So they played this out very, very slowly.
What Tim Cook has done, and I do think this is going to change in the Ternus era as we progress here, is that he came up with this strategy that I call “Hotel California.” You never want to leave. Tim Cook, he’s staying around as executive chairman. The general counsel had her stay around an extra six to nine months to run government affairs. Jeff Williams stayed around three to four months after stepping down as COO to just oversee the design team, the watch team, and the health teams as part of a transition.
For CFO Luca Maestri, the vast majority of his responsibilities went to his successor, but he kept three things. He kept oversight of information systems and technology. It’s basically like your IT department, corporate information security — which is security for the organization — and corporate real estate, so campuses, retail stores, facilities, and whatnot. It was kind of a BS job, I’ll be honest with you.
It was more so keeping him on the payroll and keeping him around in case things hit the fan, they had a financial issue, and they needed the adult or the grandfather in the room to take the bull by the horns and fix things as they transitioned to the new guy. But now Luca, he’s still there, still getting paid, and he’s teaching a class once a week at Apple University. So he’s a professor there now. I’m not sure how much longer that’s going to run for, but he’s still there.
All these old-school Apple guys are either retired or semi-retired or a notch between semi-retirement and retirement. And then we have Phil Schiller. The same week that Ternus took over as CEO, I reported that Schiller is leaving his remaining responsibilities of running the App Store and running Apple Events, and he’s at Apple now for the next little while working on special projects. They’re not saying what that is, but he’s there, reporting to Ternus, and still on the Apple leadership website. He’s around if needed in sort of an advisory capacity, and we’ll see how long that lasts.
But really this is just a gigantic end-to-end change of the guard at Apple. It’s the biggest executive overhaul I’ve certainly seen in my career reporting on Apple. Don’t forget, when Tim Cook took over for Steve Jobs, there was no overhaul. Many of the guys under Cook were the same guys under Jobs. So a lot of them have been there for a while. 
This is definitely a new era, a new generation, and you’re going to see more changes. The head of marketing, the head of retail, some of the other people, they’re in their mid-60s, almost. They’ve got hundreds of millions of dollars. They can’t do this forever. They’re talking internally about retirement. So you’re going to see another wave of changes in the next few years as well, I believe.
You mentioned Phil Schiller, who I’ve known for ages at Apple because I’m old. He’s transitioning out of his role running the App Store. And you had a piece of reporting that suggests part of it is because John Ternus and Eddy Cue want to extract even more money from developers. They want to keep that Apple tax high. They want to find more ways to have services revenue, and Schiller wasn’t interested in that. 
Schiller has famously always thought that Apple was squeezing its developers too much. There’s reporting; there are emails from some of these lawsuits. What’s going on there?
Yeah, it’s very interesting. I mean, obviously one part of it is that Schiller is 66. He wants to spend more time with his family, but for real, when it comes to him, he wants to do more philanthropy. He’s been involved in all sorts of stuff in that regard. But at the same time, this is a new era for Apple. Eddy Cue has a firm grip over all Apple services now, really for the first time in a while.
John Ternus is very close with Eddy Cue, and they are looking at new ways to make more money on the App Store, whether that’s additional advertising slots or additional subscription opportunities. Obviously, there’s going to be a reinvention of the App Store coming in the next few years to make more use of AI and to fill in to Siri AI as well.
Phil Schiller, according to my reporting, believes regulators are still hot on Apple’s trail. Developers are still unhappy with Apple. As they go into this new generation, he wants to distance a little bit from it, but he still loves Apple more than anything, and he’s still part of Apple for the foreseeable future.
To be clear, there was no big blow-up or anything between him, Eddy Cue, and Ternus or anything like that. It just, with all these considerations, felt like a natural time for him to step off. And he’s also stepping away from Apple events, right?
So it’s not just dropping the App Store; it’s dropping his two remaining responsibilities, which was a lot, right? He was part of the Hotel California crew, but he had the most responsibility between the App Store and Apple Events. Those are big things.
Yeah, and worth noting, he’s not wrong about the regulators. There’s still an outstanding Department of Justice antitrust case against Apple regarding the App Store, CarPlay, and all this other stuff that was started under the Biden administration and has not gone away in the Trump administration.
First of all, it’s surprising that it hasn’t gone away under the Trump administration, given the alliance between Donald Trump and Tim Cook. That has always been shocking to me. I thought that was going to get blown up a year ago.
And then the other thing is nobody knows any of this more than Schiller because he’s the one at the center of every meeting. He’s the one doing the depositions. He’s the one on the stand. So if anyone has the pulse of these governments and the pulse of developers, it’s him.
The big Decoder trope is that the structure of a company is connected directly to its culture. If you tell me how your company is roughly organized, I can tell you where about 80 percent of your problems are and where the other 20 percent of the magic is. 
Every now and again, I get pushback on this from a CEO who says, “No, no, it doesn’t matter. It’s all about the people.” I feel like Apple is both, right? The structure of Apple has been the same for a long time. Steve Jobs used to call it the world’s biggest startup. And then you just had these people who had been there forever. They’re just the same cast of characters under Cook as they were under Jobs. 
You could probably shuffle them any way you wanted, but it was the same people, and so, of course, the culture persisted. You’re describing a wholesale turnover at the top. And then it also seems like there are some structural changes happening underneath John Ternus, right? Jony Ive was the chief design officer of the company, which always felt to me like part of that Hotel California strategy. 
Oh, that was its own… That was like Hotel Cupertino. I mean, that was its own level.
But they were afraid of him leaving because he was so tied to the Jobs era, and then they managed to work him out of the company. We can talk about OpenAI in a bit. But Johny Srouji is the chief hardware officer now. That’s not a title Apple has ever had before. That also feels like potentially a transitional title.
Can we talk about that? Can we talk about Srouji for a minute?
Yeah.
Right now, Srouji is the second most important person at Apple. He created Apple Silicon. And let’s just face it: you cover the whole industry, I cover the whole industry; that’s their key differentiator. That’s what allows them to do different stuff. That’s their competitive advantage. Letting this guy walk out the door would’ve been a nightmare scenario, especially right now.
Last fall, really late summer to early fall, he goes to Tim Cook and tells him he’s done. This is right when planning for Ternus taking over is kicking into high gear. Tim says, “I need you to stick around as part of the transition. We can’t have you go elsewhere. We can’t have you go to Nvidia,” or wherever he was thinking about going. Certainly not retiring. This guy’s not ready to retire, I don’t think. 
So Tim says, “Here’s what we’ll do. When Ternus becomes CEO, we’ll make you chief hardware officer. So you’re going to keep your existing team, and then you’re going to get all the Ternus stuff, and then you’ll undoubtedly be the second most important person at Apple.” Srouji agrees, takes a new pay package, I’m sure, and now is in that chief hardware officer role.
I do not believe that is a long-term thing. I think that he’s already back to wanting to transition to something new, to transition out of Apple. He really has not a lot left to do. He conquered the Mac; he dumped Intel; he dumped Qualcomm. What’s left? This is a guy who wants new challenges and new things, and he’s done it all at Apple, and there’s no next thing to go after. They’ve really done it all. 
So it’ll be interesting to see how quickly that happens, I think in a year or two. And then when that happens, this recombination of the hardware engineering teams into one group, they’re going to have to break that up again because there’s no successor to Srouji who has that industry clout and that leadership capability to be a singular hardware figurehead at the company.
Yeah, if you have managed to acquire Intel’s disastrous modem business and fix it, what worlds left are there to conquer?
Exactly.
It was the hardest thing you could have possibly wanted to do, and he did it. Those modems are shipping in the new phones.
And no complaints, right? If I were to place a bet with you two years ago, how is this Apple modem thing going to go? I would’ve guessed it was going to be a disaster.
Well, they did have to slow down the Qualcomm modems to make their modems look competitive.
Fine, but-
There is certain stuff in there for sure.
Fine. But I’m talking about articles, about people’s calls dropping, not being able to load webpages and whatnot. All things considered, pretty seamless.
True. So this is the question that I’m really getting at: we’re talking about a lot of new people and, inside of it, a return to form in terms of just what that leadership page looks like. There’s no chief design officer who’s a legend in his own right. You’re saying soon there won’t be a chief hardware officer who’s a legend in his own right. 
Of the heads of design listed on that page, Alan Dye left and went to Meta. Now they’re just vice presidents again. They’re not even SVPs of design, but they report to John Ternus. We’re headed back towards a more functional Apple. They’ve gotten to some kind of divisional structure as they try to keep all these powerful people. What do you think that’s going to do to the company, or is that just going to be more of the same?
It’s so interesting. You look at the number of things and the amount of stuff that each of these reports that John Ternus has; it’s a lot. I also think you have a problem where there are vice presidents, so a tier below the SVPs, who want to grow, but you have these senior VPs who are going to be there forever, like Eddy Cue. 
He’s been there for almost four decades. And you’ve had people under Eddy Cue who’ve left for newer jobs and big things outside of the company because they wanted to replace Eddy internally, but they know that he’s never leaving. They knew that he was going to stick around for a long time. So you’re losing good people at the VP level.
I think, eventually, you’re going to see an additional layer. I think you’re going to see this chief hardware officer idea become some new thing they’re going to try. For example, could they make Craig Federighi, who runs software, like chief software and AI officer or something at one point, and then elevate some of the people under him to that senior VP level, give them more responsibility, give them more money to keep more people around? 
So I think that leadership structure is going to be in flux for a while until they figure out how to do this. I mean, the old, old Apple, they had VPs, they had senior VPs, they had executive VPs. You can imagine they’re going to play with these things in order to keep people, because I think one of their biggest problems, other than AI at this point, is retention of key players.
I actually would draw the connection between retention and AI. Not having that bench of younger people with new ideas or disruptive ideas, I think, prevented them from seeing AI for what it was.
That’s a really good point.
I think about what came to be known as the Cook Doctrine, where Tim Cook would often say, “We want to own and control every foundational technology that goes into our phones.” This is really just a statement of Apple’s own paranoia about being chained to Intel for a long time or whatever it might be.
